clinicalPearls: A delusional misidentification syndrome in which the patient believes that a familiar persecutor is disguising themselves as various strangers encountered in daily life.

Characterised by hyperidentification: unfamiliar people are misidentified as one known individual despite no physical resemblance, sometimes described as psychological identity without physical identity.
Named after Leopoldo Fregoli, an Italian quick-change stage performer famed for rapid transformations of appearance.
Contrasts with the Capgras delusion, in which a familiar person is believed to have been replaced by an impostor.
Associated with paranoid schizophrenia but also with right frontal and temporal lobe pathology, dementia, and traumatic brain injury.
Usually embedded within persecutory delusions, with the disguised figure experienced as a stalker or persecutor.
Neuropsychological accounts implicate dysfunction of face-recognition and familiarity-monitoring networks involving the fusiform and right frontal regions.
Late onset, cognitive impairment, or absence of other psychotic features should prompt thorough organic screening.
reference.pathophysiology: Fregoli syndrome is conceptualised as a disorder of person identification arising from disrupted integration between face-recognition pathways and the affective and mnemonic systems that assign familiarity. Whereas Capgras is linked to loss of the normal autonomic familiarity response, Fregoli is thought to reflect excessive or misattributed familiarity, so that strangers evoke recognition of a known person. Right frontal and temporal dysfunction impairs the monitoring and belief-evaluation processes that would normally reject such misidentifications, allowing the delusion to persist. It occurs both in primary psychotic illness, notably schizophrenia with dopaminergic dysregulation, and in structural or neurodegenerative brain disease.
additionalInvestigations: Structural neuroimaging (MRI brain) to identify right frontotemporal pathology
Cognitive and neuropsychological testing including face recognition
EEG where seizure activity or delirium is suspected
Organic screen bloods (full blood count, metabolic panel, thyroid function, calcium, vitamin B12)
Collateral history to establish onset, content, and progression
CSF analysis and autoimmune encephalitis antibodies if atypical or rapidly progressive
redFlags: Late-onset misidentification with cognitive decline suggesting neurodegeneration
Focal neurological signs pointing to a structural lesion
Persecutory content directed at a specific person, raising risk of violence
Rapid progression with fluctuating consciousness suggesting encephalitis or delirium
reference.prognosis: Outcome largely follows the underlying disorder; misidentification in schizophrenia often improves with antipsychotic treatment, whereas that due to neurodegenerative disease tends to persist or progress.
pitfalls: Assuming a primary psychiatric cause without excluding organic or neurodegenerative disease
Overlooking the risk of violence toward the misidentified persecutor
Confusing Fregoli (hyperidentification of strangers as one known person) with Capgras
Failing to obtain collateral history that reveals the delusional structure
references: Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry
management: Treatment of the underlying disorder, with antipsychotic medication when the misidentification arises from schizophrenia or another primary psychosis
Identification and management of any underlying organic or neurodegenerative cause such as right frontotemporal pathology, dementia or traumatic brain injury, directing treatment accordingly
Risk assessment and safety planning given the persecutory content, as the misidentified figure may be experienced as a threatening stalker
Cognitive support with dementia-directed therapy such as cholinesterase inhibitors where a neurodegenerative process is responsible
Multidisciplinary care coordinating psychiatry and neurology, with carer support and psychoeducation
Longitudinal follow-up to monitor treatment response and progression of the underlying disease
